You are comparing two drafts written from the same brief. Read no other file, and do not run commands or browse; judge only the text below.

Brief: Write the README's opening paragraph and its Install and update section for the `tidy-hooks` plugin.

<<<DRAFT A
`tidy-hooks` is a Claude and Codex plugin that blocks `git commit` when staged files contain merge markers. If Node.js is missing, the hook lets commits proceed.

## Install and update

### Claude

Add the marketplace, then install the plugin:

```sh
claude plugin marketplace add example/tidy
claude plugin install tidy-hooks@tidy
```

To update:

```sh
claude plugin update tidy-hooks@tidy
```

### Codex

Add the marketplace, then install the plugin:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add example/tidy
codex plugin add tidy-hooks@tidy
```

Review and trust the plugin hooks. Codex skips them until you do.

To update:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace upgrade tidy
```

Then restart Codex.
DRAFT A>>>

items.title: Thinking
items.text:
I'm comparing the two versions side by side. One says the hook lets commits proceed, while the other just says commits proceed. The trust step sits after install in one, which is the right order, since you install first and then review and trust. The other puts the warning ahead of install as a note, so it implies an action without spelling it out as a step.

I'm weighing the two versions on how clearly they tell the reader what to do. The first one puts the trust step right after install, which is the sensible order, and it's phrased as a direct instruction. The second raises the caveat before any steps, which is also defensible, though it leaves the action implied rather than stated. I'm leaning toward the first overall.
